title: Harper Argues Against the Multi-System Stack and Releases 5.2
gist: Database platform Harper published a benchmark arguing its single-runtime, code-and-data-colocated architecture beats a Vercel/Neon/Upstash/Ably stack on live personalized-data workloads by several-fold to ~14x, while conceding Vercel's serverless autoscaling wins under high fan-out load and that its own headline benchmark predates the 5.2 release it just shipped.

themes.theme: Harper's collapsed-layer thesis versus the decoupling trend

insights.claim: Harper's architecture runs counter to a trend InfoQ covered with Databricks' Lakebase, which separates compute from storage: where Lakebase bets on decoupling layers, Harper bets on collapsing database, cache, and job runner into a single runtime for operational simplicity and cost advantages.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Frames a live architectural debate in the data-platform market between disaggregation (Lakebase) and colocation (Harper) — useful for positioning either camp against a given workload's read latency and freshness requirements.
insights.locator: The approach runs counter to a trend InfoQ covered in February

insights.claim: Harper's own benchmark measured in-process data access at roughly 0.4ms versus a roughly 3ms network hop to a separate tier in a typical multi-system stack, with the gap widening as a page pulls in more personalized data elements.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A concrete latency delta (0.4ms vs ~3ms per hop) that compounds on pages with many personalized data calls, quantifying the core claim behind Harper's colocation pitch.
insights.locator: Its own benchmark against a Vercel-based stack measured in-process data access

insights.claim: Harper's benchmark built the same emoji product-catalog application twice behind a single shared DataSource contract — once on Harper with data, compute, and messaging co-located, once on a Vercel stack wiring together Vercel Functions, Neon Postgres, Upstash Redis, and Ably for real-time — running 474 load tests across eight scenarios and two US regions over three trials.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A controlled same-app, same-contract methodology (rather than comparing unrelated apps) makes the resulting latency deltas more directly attributable to the architecture rather than implementation differences.
insights.quote: We built one identical app twice. Once inside Harper, once on Vercel with Neon, Upstash, and Ably. Same UI, same code contract, same data. The only variable was the architecture.

insights.claim: The benchmark outcome is explicitly workload-dependent: under high, sustained fan-out load, Vercel's serverless autoscaling outperforms Harper's single free-node configuration, which hits a throughput ceiling as concurrency increases, while live data favors Harper's co-located runtime and cache-heavy edge delivery favors the serverless stack.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Undercuts a simple 'Harper is faster' takeaway — the architecture choice should be workload-matched (live/personalized reads vs. high-fan-out cacheable content) rather than treated as a universal winner.
insights.locator: Under a high, sustained fan-out load, Vercel's serverless autoscaling outperforms Harper's single free node

insights.claim: Harper's co-located, in-process architecture wins every live, personalized-data path tested — single reads, injected live values, server-side streaming, write-to-read freshness, and read fan-out at normal load — often several-fold and up to roughly 14x, symmetrically across both US coasts, while Vercel wins cacheable content delivery and broadcast-only realtime.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Quantifies the specific workload class (live, personalized, write-to-read-fresh data) where a colocated runtime like Harper offers the largest measured advantage, useful for architecture selection on personalization-heavy products.
insights.quote: Harper's co-located, in-process architecture wins every live, personalized-data path — single reads, injected live values, server-side streaming, write-to-read freshness, and read fan-out at normal load — often several-fold, up to ~14×, and symmetrically across coasts. Vercel wins cacheable content (its CDN is superb) and broadcast-only realtime.

insights.claim: The benchmark uses a warm, in-memory dataset, and the article notes Harper's advantage may narrow once the working set exceeds available memory — a caveat on how far the several-fold-to-14x results generalize to larger, colder datasets.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A direct limitation to weigh before extrapolating the benchmark's headline multipliers to production datasets that don't fit in memory.
insights.locator: The benchmark uses a warm, in-memory dataset

themes.theme: Harper 5.2 release and an unrefreshed benchmark

insights.claim: Harper 5.2 adds a record cache that the company says serves repeated reads five to eight times faster, and gives each database its own commit path so heavy writes no longer stall unrelated work in the same process.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A concrete throughput-per-node improvement independent of the Vercel comparison, relevant to teams already running Harper and evaluating an upgrade.

insights.claim: The 5.2 fix addressed database commits sharing Node's libuv worker pool with unrelated filesystem work in earlier versions; isolating commit paths dropped the p99 latency of an unrelated filesystem call from 223.7ms to 2.6ms.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A striking concrete before/after number (223.7ms to 2.6ms p99) illustrating how shared-runtime designs like Harper's can suffer noisy-neighbor effects if internal resource isolation is done wrong — and how much isolating them can help.
insights.locator: database commits sharing Node’s libuv worker pool

insights.claim: Harper's benchmark against the Vercel stack predates the 5.2 release and has not been re-run since, meaning the widely cited several-fold-to-14x performance claims do not yet reflect the record cache or commit-isolation improvements just shipped.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A material caveat for anyone citing Harper's benchmark numbers as current: the underlying product has already changed since the numbers were measured, likely in Harper's favor.
insights.quote: Harper’s benchmark predates version 5.2 and has not been re-run.
insights.locator: Harper’s benchmark predates version 5.2 and has not been re-run.

themes.theme: Architectural framing: reads as in-process function calls

insights.claim: Harper's GTM lead Aleks Haugom frames the architecture's core idea as: a personalized read is not a network request to another service but a function call against an in-memory table, with the data unit replicated to a node in every region and kept globally in sync so each user is served in-process by the nearest node while still seeing consistent data.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Articulates the specific mechanism (per-region replicated in-memory tables) behind Harper's latency claims, useful for evaluating whether the same approach fits a given team's consistency and freshness requirements.
insights.quote: A personalized read is not a network request to another service; it is a function call against an in-memory table.
insights.locator: discusses different architectures for web personalization
